lessons.title: SELECT & FROM
lessons.description: Retrieve data from tables — your first SQL statement
lessons.theory_md:
## SELECT & FROM

SQL retrieves data using SELECT and FROM.

```sql
SELECT column1, column2 FROM table_name;
SELECT * FROM table_name;  -- all columns
```

**Key rules:**
- `*` means all columns
- Column names separated by commas
- Semicolon ends the statement
- SQL is case-insensitive (convention: KEYWORDS uppercase)

**Business context:** Every report starts here. You're telling the database exactly what information to return.

lessons.title: ORDER BY & LIMIT
lessons.description: Sort results and retrieve top N records
lessons.theory_md:
## ORDER BY

Sorts query results.

```sql
SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY age;          -- ASC default
SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY age DESC;     -- descending
SELECT * FROM patients ORDER BY ward, age;    -- multiple columns
```

**Top N pattern** — used in nearly every business report:
```sql
SELECT patient_name, age FROM patients
ORDER BY age DESC
LIMIT 10;  -- top 10 oldest
```

**Business context:** 'Top 10 customers', 'Most expensive procedures', 'Oldest open tickets' — all ORDER BY + LIMIT.

lessons.title: GROUP BY & Aggregations
lessons.description: Summarize data by category — the heart of analytical SQL
lessons.theory_md:
## GROUP BY & Aggregate Functions

Group rows and compute summaries per group.

**Aggregate functions:**
```sql
COUNT(*)          -- count rows
COUNT(column)     -- count non-null values
SUM(column)       -- total
AVG(column)       -- average
MAX(column)       -- maximum
MIN(column)       -- minimum
ROUND(value, 2)   -- round to 2 decimal places
```

**Pattern:**
```sql
SELECT category, COUNT(*) as count
FROM table
GROUP BY category
ORDER BY count DESC;
```

**Golden rule:** Every column in SELECT must either be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate function.

**Business context:** KPIs are GROUP BY queries. 'Revenue by region', 'Patients by diagnosis', 'Orders by month' — all of these.

exercises.hint_2: Add ORDER BY patient_count DESC at the end.
exercises.hint_3: SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as patient_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward ORDER BY patient_count DESC
exercises.solution: SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as patient_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward ORDER BY patient_count DESC

exercises.hint_2: SELECT gender, ROUND(AVG(age), 1) as avg_age FROM patients GROUP BY gender
exercises.hint_3: SELECT gender, ROUND(AVG(age), 1) as avg_age FROM patients GROUP BY gender

exercises.hint_3: SELECT diagnosis, SUM(bill_amount) as total_revenue FROM billing GROUP BY diagnosis ORDER BY total_revenue DESC
exercises.solution: SELECT diagnosis, SUM(bill_amount) as total_revenue FROM billing GROUP BY diagnosis ORDER BY total_revenue DESC

exercises.hint_3: SELECT ward, MIN(age) as min_age, MAX(age) as max_age FROM patients GROUP BY ward

lessons.title: HAVING Clause
lessons.description: Filter aggregated results — WHERE for GROUP BY
lessons.theory_md:
## HAVING

HAVING filters groups after aggregation. WHERE filters rows before aggregation.

```sql
-- WHERE: filters rows BEFORE grouping
SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as cnt
FROM patients
WHERE gender = 'Female'   -- filter rows first
GROUP BY ward
HAVING cnt > 10;          -- then filter groups
```

**Rule:** Use WHERE for column conditions. Use HAVING for aggregate conditions.

**Business context:** 'Show me only regions with sales > 100,000' — that's HAVING, not WHERE.

exercises.title: Wards with Many Patients
exercises.prompt: Find wards with more than 30 patients. Return ward and patient_count.
exercises.hint_1: GROUP BY ward, then use HAVING COUNT(*) > 30
exercises.hint_2: SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as patient_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward HAVING patient_count > 30
exercises.hint_3: SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as patient_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward HAVING COUNT(*) > 30
exercises.solution: SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as patient_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward HAVING COUNT(*) > 30

exercises.title: High Revenue Diagnoses
exercises.prompt: Find diagnoses with total billing over 500,000. Return diagnosis and total_billed.
exercises.hint_1: SUM(bill_amount) > 500000 goes in HAVING, not WHERE.
exercises.hint_2: SELECT diagnosis, SUM(bill_amount) as total_billed FROM billing GROUP BY diagnosis HAVING total_billed > 500000
exercises.hint_3: SELECT diagnosis, SUM(bill_amount) as total_billed FROM billing GROUP BY diagnosis HAVING SUM(bill_amount) > 500000 ORDER BY total_billed DESC
exercises.solution: SELECT diagnosis, SUM(bill_amount) as total_billed FROM billing GROUP BY diagnosis HAVING SUM(bill_amount) > 500000 ORDER BY total_billed DESC

exercises.title: WHERE and HAVING Together

exercises.hint_1: Use WHERE gender = 'Female' to filter rows, then HAVING AVG(age) > 45 to filter groups.
exercises.hint_2: SELECT ward, ROUND(AVG(age),1) as avg_age FROM patients WHERE gender = 'Female' GROUP BY ward HAVING AVG(age) > 45
exercises.hint_3: SELECT ward, ROUND(AVG(age),1) as avg_age FROM patients WHERE gender = 'Female' GROUP BY ward HAVING AVG(age) > 45 ORDER BY avg_age DESC
exercises.solution: SELECT ward, ROUND(AVG(age),1) as avg_age FROM patients WHERE gender = 'Female' GROUP BY ward HAVING AVG(age) > 45 ORDER BY avg_age DESC

lessons.title: JOINs
lessons.theory_md:
## JOINs

Real databases split data across tables. JOINs combine them.

**INNER JOIN** — only matched rows:
```sql
SELECT p.patient_name, b.bill_amount
FROM patients p
INNER JOIN billing b ON p.patient_id = b.patient_id;
```

**LEFT JOIN** — all left rows, NULL where no match:
```sql
SELECT p.patient_name, b.bill_amount
FROM patients p
LEFT JOIN billing b ON p.patient_id = b.patient_id;
-- patients with no bill get NULL for bill_amount
```

**Aliases** (p, b) keep queries readable.

**Business context:** Most reports require 3-5 tables. A patient report needs patients + billing + diagnoses. Mastering JOINs is the defining skill of a working analyst.

lessons.title: Subqueries
lessons.description: Queries inside queries — powerful multi-step logic
lessons.theory_md:
## Subqueries

A subquery is a query nested inside another query.

**In WHERE:**
```sql
-- Patients older than the average age
SELECT patient_name, age
FROM patients
WHERE age > (SELECT AVG(age) FROM patients);
```

**In FROM (derived table):**
```sql
SELECT ward, avg_age
FROM (
  SELECT ward, AVG(age) as avg_age
  FROM patients
  GROUP BY ward
) ward_stats
WHERE avg_age > 40;
```

**With IN:**
```sql
-- Patients who have a billing record
SELECT patient_name
FROM patients
WHERE patient_id IN (
  SELECT DISTINCT patient_id FROM billing
);
```

**Business context:** Subqueries answer multi-step questions: 'Show me only the top-performing wards' where 'top-performing' itself requires a calculation.

exercises.title: Above Average Age
exercises.prompt: Find patients older than the average patient age. Return patient_name and age.
exercises.hint_1: WHERE age > (SELECT AVG(age) FROM patients)
exercises.hint_2: SELECT patient_name, age FROM patients WHERE age > (SELECT AVG(age) FROM patients)
exercises.hint_3: SELECT patient_name, age FROM patients WHERE age > (SELECT AVG(age) FROM patients) ORDER BY age DESC
exercises.solution: SELECT patient_name, age FROM patients WHERE age > (SELECT AVG(age) FROM patients) ORDER BY age DESC

exercises.title: Subquery in FROM
exercises.prompt: Calculate the average bill amount per ward (via patient join), then show only wards with avg_bill above 20000.
exercises.hint_1: First write a subquery that calculates avg bill per ward, then wrap it in SELECT ... WHERE avg_bill > 20000.
exercises.hint_2: SELECT ward, avg_bill FROM (SELECT p.ward, AVG(b.bill_amount) as avg_bill FROM patients p JOIN billing b ON p.patient_id = b.patient_id GROUP BY p.ward) t WHERE avg_bill > 20000
exercises.hint_3: SELECT ward, avg_bill FROM (SELECT p.ward, ROUND(AVG(b.bill_amount),2) as avg_bill FROM patients p JOIN billing b ON p.patient_id = b.patient_id GROUP BY p.ward) t WHERE avg_bill > 20000 ORDER BY avg_bill DESC
exercises.solution: SELECT ward, avg_bill FROM (SELECT p.ward, ROUND(AVG(b.bill_amount),2) as avg_bill FROM patients p JOIN billing b ON p.patient_id = b.patient_id GROUP BY p.ward) t WHERE avg_bill > 20000 ORDER BY avg_bill DESC

lessons.title: CTEs (WITH clause)
lessons.theory_md:
## Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

CTEs are named subqueries defined before the main query using WITH. They make complex queries readable.

```sql
WITH ward_stats AS (
  SELECT ward,
         COUNT(*) as patient_count,
         AVG(age) as avg_age
  FROM patients
  GROUP BY ward
)
SELECT *
FROM ward_stats
WHERE patient_count > 20
ORDER BY avg_age DESC;
```

**Multiple CTEs:**
```sql
WITH
admitted AS (
  SELECT * FROM patients WHERE discharge_date IS NULL
),
high_risk AS (
  SELECT * FROM admitted WHERE age > 65
)
SELECT * FROM high_risk;
```

**Business context:** CTEs are how professional analysts structure complex queries — each step is named, readable, and reusable in the same query.

exercises.title: Your First CTE
exercises.prompt: Use a CTE named ward_summary to calculate patient count per ward, then select only wards with more than 25 patients from it.
exercises.hint_1: WITH ward_summary AS (SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM patients GROUP BY ward) SELECT ...
exercises.hint_2: WITH ward_summary AS (SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM patients GROUP BY ward) SELECT * FROM ward_summary WHERE cnt > 25
exercises.hint_3: WITH ward_summary AS (SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM patients GROUP BY ward) SELECT ward, cnt FROM ward_summary WHERE cnt > 25 ORDER BY cnt DESC
exercises.solution: WITH ward_summary AS (SELECT ward, COUNT(*) as cnt FROM patients GROUP BY ward) SELECT ward, cnt FROM ward_summary WHERE cnt > 25 ORDER BY cnt DESC

exercises.title: Chained CTEs
exercises.prompt: Write two CTEs: 'still_admitted' (patients with no discharge date), and 'elderly_admitted' (from still_admitted where age > 60). Return patient_name, ward, age from elderly_admitted.
exercises.hint_1: WITH still_admitted AS (...), elderly_admitted AS (SELECT * FROM still_admitted WHERE age > 60)
exercises.hint_2: WITH still_admitted AS (SELECT * FROM patients WHERE discharge_date IS NULL), elderly_admitted AS (SELECT * FROM still_admitted WHERE age > 60) SELECT patient_name, ward, age FROM elderly_admitted
exercises.hint_3: WITH still_admitted AS (SELECT * FROM patients WHERE discharge_date IS NULL), elderly_admitted AS (SELECT * FROM still_admitted WHERE age > 60) SELECT patient_name, ward, age FROM elderly_admitted ORDER BY age DESC
exercises.solution: WITH still_admitted AS (SELECT * FROM patients WHERE discharge_date IS NULL), elderly_admitted AS (SELECT * FROM still_admitted WHERE age > 60) SELECT patient_name, ward, age FROM elderly_admitted ORDER BY age DESC

lessons.title: Window Functions
lessons.description: RANK, ROW_NUMBER, LAG, running totals — advanced analytical queries
lessons.theory_md:
## Window Functions

Window functions compute values across a set of rows related to the current row — without collapsing rows like GROUP BY.

```sql
function() OVER (
  PARTITION BY column   -- group within
  ORDER BY column       -- order within group
)
```

**Ranking:**
```sql
ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC)
RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY bill_amount DESC)  -- gaps on tie
DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY bill_amount DESC)  -- no gaps
```

**Lag/Lead (compare to adjacent rows):**
```sql
LAG(bill_amount, 1) OVER (PARTITION BY patient_id ORDER BY bill_date)
LEAD(bill_amount, 1) OVER (ORDER BY bill_date)
```

**Running totals:**
```sql
SUM(bill_amount) OVER (ORDER BY bill_date) as running_total
```

**Business context:** Month-over-month growth, running totals, customer ranking, top N per group — all window functions.

exercises.title: Rank by Age in Ward
exercises.prompt: Rank patients within each ward by age (oldest = rank 1). Return patient_name, ward, age, and age_rank.
exercises.hint_1: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC) as age_rank
exercises.hint_2: SELECT patient_name, ward, age, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC) as age_rank FROM patients
exercises.hint_3: SELECT patient_name, ward, age, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC) as age_rank FROM patients ORDER BY ward, age_rank
exercises.solution: SELECT patient_name, ward, age, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC) as age_rank FROM patients ORDER BY ward, age_rank

exercises.title: Running Total of Bills
exercises.prompt: Show each billing record with a running total of bill_amount ordered by bill_date. Return bill_id, bill_date, bill_amount, and running_total.
exercises.hint_1: SUM(bill_amount) OVER (ORDER BY bill_date) as running_total
exercises.hint_2: SELECT bill_id, bill_date, bill_amount, SUM(bill_amount) OVER (ORDER BY bill_date) as running_total FROM billing
exercises.hint_3: SELECT bill_id, bill_date, bill_amount, ROUND(SUM(bill_amount) OVER (ORDER BY bill_date), 2) as running_total FROM billing ORDER BY bill_date
exercises.solution: SELECT bill_id, bill_date, bill_amount, ROUND(SUM(bill_amount) OVER (ORDER BY bill_date), 2) as running_total FROM billing ORDER BY bill_date

exercises.title: Top 3 per Ward
exercises.prompt: Find the top 3 oldest patients in each ward using ROW_NUMBER. Return only rows where row_num <= 3.
exercises.hint_1: Use a CTE with ROW_NUMBER, then filter WHERE row_num <= 3.
exercises.hint_2: WITH ranked AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC) as row_num FROM patients) SELECT patient_name, ward, age FROM ranked WHERE row_num <= 3
exercises.hint_3: WITH ranked AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC) as row_num FROM patients) SELECT patient_name, ward, age, row_num FROM ranked WHERE row_num <= 3 ORDER BY ward, row_num
exercises.solution: WITH ranked AS (SELECT *, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ward ORDER BY age DESC) as row_num FROM patients) SELECT patient_name, ward, age, row_num FROM ranked WHERE row_num <= 3 ORDER BY ward, row_num

lessons.title: CASE WHEN
lessons.description: Conditional logic inside queries — build categories on the fly
lessons.theory_md:
## CASE WHEN

CASE WHEN adds conditional logic directly inside SQL — like IF/ELSE.

```sql
SELECT patient_name, age,
  CASE
    WHEN age < 18 THEN 'Pediatric'
    WHEN age BETWEEN 18 AND 60 THEN 'Adult'
    ELSE 'Senior'
  END as age_group
FROM patients;
```

**In aggregations:**
```sql
SELECT
  COUNT(CASE WHEN gender = 'Male' THEN 1 END) as male_count,
  COUNT(CASE WHEN gender = 'Female' THEN 1 END) as female_count
FROM patients;
```

**Business context:** Categorizing continuous data (age groups, revenue tiers, risk levels), pivoting rows to columns, conditional counts.

exercises.title: Age Groups

exercises.hint_1: Use CASE WHEN age < 18 THEN 'Child' WHEN age <= 60 THEN 'Adult' ELSE 'Senior' END as age_group
exercises.hint_2: SELECT patient_name, age, CASE WHEN age < 18 THEN 'Child' WHEN age BETWEEN 18 AND 60 THEN 'Adult' ELSE 'Senior' END as age_group FROM patients
exercises.hint_3: SELECT patient_name, age, CASE WHEN age < 18 THEN 'Child' WHEN age BETWEEN 18 AND 60 THEN 'Adult' ELSE 'Senior' END as age_group FROM patients
exercises.solution: SELECT patient_name, age, CASE WHEN age < 18 THEN 'Child' WHEN age BETWEEN 18 AND 60 THEN 'Adult' ELSE 'Senior' END as age_group FROM patients

exercises.title: Bill Risk Tier
exercises.prompt: From billing, classify each bill: under 10000 = 'Low', 10000-50000 = 'Medium', above 50000 = 'High'. Return bill_id, bill_amount, and risk_tier.
exercises.hint_1: CASE WHEN bill_amount < 10000 THEN 'Low' WHEN bill_amount <= 50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'High' END
exercises.hint_2: SELECT bill_id, bill_amount, CASE WHEN bill_amount < 10000 THEN 'Low' WHEN bill_amount <= 50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'High' END as risk_tier FROM billing
exercises.hint_3: SELECT bill_id, bill_amount, CASE WHEN bill_amount < 10000 THEN 'Low' WHEN bill_amount <= 50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'High' END as risk_tier FROM billing
exercises.solution: SELECT bill_id, bill_amount, CASE WHEN bill_amount < 10000 THEN 'Low' WHEN bill_amount <= 50000 THEN 'Medium' ELSE 'High' END as risk_tier FROM billing

exercises.title: Conditional Count
exercises.prompt: Count male and female patients per ward in a single query using conditional aggregation. Return ward, male_count, female_count.
exercises.hint_1: COUNT(CASE WHEN gender = 'Male' THEN 1 END) counts only males.
exercises.hint_2: SELECT ward, COUNT(CASE WHEN gender='Male' THEN 1 END) as male_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN gender='Female' THEN 1 END) as female_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward
exercises.hint_3: SELECT ward, COUNT(CASE WHEN gender='Male' THEN 1 END) as male_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN gender='Female' THEN 1 END) as female_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward ORDER BY ward
exercises.solution: SELECT ward, COUNT(CASE WHEN gender='Male' THEN 1 END) as male_count, COUNT(CASE WHEN gender='Female' THEN 1 END) as female_count FROM patients GROUP BY ward ORDER BY ward
